The reply was a volley of shots, the sheriff returning the fire and emptying his revolver. Before he could reload, he was shot down by the mob, one shot taking effect in his right leg above the knee and another in his pistol arm, thereby disabling him.

His daughter, Miss Ola Austin, ran to her father, and was at once covered by a pistol in the hands of one of the mob, and made to surrender the keys.

WOUNDS NOT SEVERE
SHERIFF AUSTIN WILL SOON BE WELL AGAIN.
Representative Citizens of Jackson County Praise Him and His Brave Daughter for Their Defense of the Negro.
Scottsboro, July 1.—(Special.)—Sheriff Austin, who was shot in the thigh and hand while resisting the mob that lynched Andy Diggs, a negro, for attempted assault on Miss Alma Smith, daughter of Dr. B. The body of the negro, after being viewed by hundreds of people, was cut down yesterday about noon and turned over to his father, Mose Diggs, and taken to Larkinsville for interment. His father is a respectable old negro and is well thought of.

The lynching of a negro in jail at Scottsboro who had confessed his base criminality in attempting a nameless crime was wholly uncalled for on any ground save that of passion. High Jackson does not contain many negroes, and there is no fear there of a troublesome race question. It is a white county, containing but 1836 negroes all told, men, women and children, in a total of 30,508. And yet in this white county, controlled in every respect by whites, a sheriff was shot down, and his brave daughters brushed aside, in order that a mob might wreak its vengeance upon a prisoner regardless, and in defiance, of all law and all order.

This is the first lynching that has occurred in this state this year, and The Age-Herald has full faith that Governor Jelks will assert the supremacy of the law, and will see that the brave sheriff of the county is himself avenged by the arrest and punishment of the ringleaders of the Larkinsville mob. The people of Scottsboro had no part in the assault upon the jail and the disabling of the sheriff, but the mob came from a remote district of the county.

Governor Jelks now has an opportunity to teach the followers of Judge Lynch a lesson they will long remembr. AT MANCHURIA STATION

RUSSIANS HAVE SETTLED AT EVERY RAILROAD TOWN.

Cannot Yet Purchase Land and Secure Titles.

Washington, Dec. 26.--According to a report received at the state department from United States Commercial Agent Greener at Vladivostock, Siberia, under date of July 25, 1903, Russian settlements have made their appearance at nearly all the larger railroad stations in Manchuria. Besides railroad offices and houses for employes, there are many private buildings. One impediment to the expansion of these settlements is that no regular sales of land have yet been arranged for. It is said that there will be an auction sale of lots next year. In the meantime, private persons are allowed to occupy lots temporarily.

Regarding the affairs of Siberia, Commercial Agent Greener says there is a surveying party now engaged in defining the route of the second Siberian railway. Pineapple, Dec. 26.—(Special.)—At 5 o'clock this morning, fire originating in the town jail, destroyed that structure, eight stores, the postoffice, two warehouses and other property in the business portion of the town. The financial loss will approximate $35,000, with insurance less than one-third that amount.

Evidence has developed that the conflagration was started by a mob. The charred body of Arthur Stewart, a negro, who wasc in the jail charged with attempted murder, was discovered in the ruins.

The negro had been killed by the mob and the jail set on fire to destroy evidence of the crime. The flames spread rapidly, owing to a high wind blowing at the time, and it is believed that the mob's members fled, seeing that their action might result in the destruction of the business section of the place.

arthur-stuart-pineapple-1903-12-26.A11:
Pineapple's Christmas Frolic.
A desire for excitement and blood was plainly at the bottom of the distressing and absolutely inexcusable lynching and conflagration that occurred at Pineapple on Christmas evening. Even the mob did not claim that their victim killed young Melton, who was shot as a result of crap playing with negroes. They simply knew that a negro had been arrested who had perhaps participated in the game of craps. They did not investigate; they did not even desire to investigate. They wanted blood, and they got it in a barbaric manner, with a conflagration thrown in that nearly destroyed the town.

This case amply illustrates the beauties of lynch law. It demonstrates the dangers of anarchy. It is a warning to all the state, and it is a warning that should not o unheeded.

If the authorities do not obey public sentiment in Pineapple itself, and public decency and the intelligence of the state, then more of the same sort may be expected in this state. Pineapple and Scottsboro furnished the two lynchings of the year in this state, and in each case punishment should be meted out to fit the crime.
arthur-stuart-pineapple-1903-12-26.A19:
Coroner's Jury Returns Sealed Verdict After Setting for Three Days
CITIZENS DETERMINED TO PUSH PROSECUTION
From Evidence Obtainable It Seems That the Negro Who Was Lynched Was Only Charged With "Presenting a Pistol."
Selma, December 29.—(Special.)—After sitting the best part of three days the coroner's jury in the investigation of the lynching of the negro and burning of over half the town of Pineapple, this afternoon brought in a sealed verdict, which was turned over to Justice of the Peace C. A. Crawford, acting as coroner.

The jury was composed of seven of the most representative citizens of Pineapple, to wit: J. M. Jackson, foreman; J. T. Adams, A. C. Luckie, J. J. Cook, J. B. Coleman, W. H. Grimes and Professor Claud Hardy.

Solicitor Quarles of the fourth circuit, who, pursuant to the request of the meeting, went to Pineapple Sunday, assisted in the labors of the jury in getting the witnesses and bringing out all the evidence possible.

The bringing in of a sealed verdict and turning it over to the justice who, under the law, if there is evidence implicating any person in the crime, may issue warrants and hand them to the sheriff for him to serve, indicates that the murder and arson has been placed upon somebody's shoulders and arrests will follow.

Citizens Are Determined.

The information received here is that the best citizens of Pineapple are determined to prosecute the matter to the fullest extent, personally and with their money.

From reliable sources it is learned that the evidence brought out before the coroner's jury was to the effect that on December 22, on the bank of a creek near the Pineapple depot, that four young white men of respectable families, Clinton Melton, known as Pig Melton, and three others, engaged in a game of craps with four negroes. Toward the end of the game a quarrel ensued, participated in by Melton and a negro named John Westley. The latter drew a pistol and in a scuffle for the weapon it was discharged accidentally, or otherwise, the ball entering the left side of Pig Melton, rang-ing downward and lodging in the left thigh and producing a painful and perhaps fatal wound.

Arthur Stewart, another negro also in the game, is claimed to have picked up his gun and walked away. Melton claims Stewart drew his gun on him, and made him let John Westley alone.

Swore Out Warrant.

On December 23, Walter Stewart, the regular constable, and a brother-in-law of Pig Melton, swore out warrants charging Westley with assault to murder, and Arthur Stewart with presenting a gun. Westley fled and has not been apprehended. Constable Stewart arrested Arthur Stewart Wednesday evening, and took him to his own home about three hundred yards from Pig Melton's home. Arthur's trial was set for Thursday by Justice of the Peace Crawford, and when the case was called it was continued indefinitely on account of Pig Melton's inability to attend.

Constable Stewart kept the negro in his custody until dark of Friday, Christmas Day, when he, in company with two others, turned the negro into the calaboose.

About 4 o'clock the next morning, with heavy clouds in the sky, and with town marshal, Payne, sick in bed, a most favorable opportunity was offered for the lynching.

Negro's Head Cracked Open.

The lock to the calaboose door was broken, the prisoner's skull cracked open like a cocoanut by a terrific blow, his body and the building saturated with kerosine and fire set to it. The evidence to all this is mostly circumstantial, but so plain as to leave no doubt of its truth.

The flames found it mere pastime to leap from the calaboose to the other buildings, and nine stores and buildings went up in smoke, the rest of the town being saved only by the heroic work of the citizens, who had no weapons, but willing hearts and hands and pails of water with which to fight.

CARRIED TO CAMDEN JAIL
Presence Was That of a
Private Citizen.

Pineapple, Jan 1.—(Special.)—After two of the justices associated to try the five men accused of the lynching of a negro confined in the Pineapple calaboose Saturday morning had declined to sit upon the case, Justice Sessions brought today's attempt at a preliminary hearing to an abrupt termination by announcing that he would not alone try the case. He said that he sat in the court, not as an officer, but as a private citizen, having neither desire to preside nor power to declare adjournment, so that the original committing magistrate, C. A. Crawford, having been disqualified yesterday, the original court is ended, not by adjournment, but, as it were, by dissolution.

The prisoners were retained in the custody of the sheriff, who escorted the men to Camden, the county seat, and the consensus is that the defendants can have reasonably early trial only by a writ of habeas corpus, which their counsel may ask, or by a special term of the court which has been requested, or Circuit Judge John Moore by State Solicitor W. W. Quarles.

The contition resultant from today's sessionsion is said to be without precedent. The disqualification of the justice before whom the warrants against the defendants were returnable, the failure of Justice Sessions's associates to act, and the declaration that an associate justice cannot associate unto himself other associates, practically annihilates the court organized to give the defendants their preliminary hearing.

Chain Not Endless.

The present status owes its being to a sort of chain that was not endless. Justice of the Peace C. A. Crawford, who acted as coroner in the inquest over the body of the negro Arthur Stewart, found murdered in the burning calaboose, was the officer to whom the warrants charging Emmet Barlow, Evander Melton, Walter C. Stewart, Robert Ray and Pressley Stewart with murder, were returnable, and at the preliminary hearing set for yesterday, when called he presided, Justices of the Peace Charles McLean and J. J. Sessions being his associates.

In the preliminary arguments of the attorneys, the counsel for the defendants objected to Mr. Crawford's serving, on the grounds that some of his property was destroyed by the fire and that he was therefore disabled.

The remaining officers, Messrs. McLean and Sessions, said that, in view of the heavy responsibility of their positions, they preferred that another justice should sit with them.

Justice of the Peace J. R. Hughes had been asked to be an associate and it was agreed that he should be the third. This morning, however, Mr. McLean did not appear in court, and asked to be excused on account of illness and Hr. Hughes thereupon declined to take upon himself more than one-third of the responsibility, saying that he would serve as one of three, but not as one of two justices, to try the case.

Mr. Sessions was thus left alone, and after a long series of arguments by the counsel of State and defense and after many questions and statements by Mr. Sessions, he stated that he would not assume the entire responsibility of a case that was not in his beat, and he brought about the remarkable existent state by saying that he did not consider himself the presiding officer of the session and that it was not in his jurisdiction to declare the court adjourned until a certain day. He was a private citizen, he said.

One by one officers filed out with the spectators and the court, as some one said, vanished in thin air, and the question. "Did they adjourn or just quit?" had no answer from justice or counsel.

Solicitor Quarles yesterday requested Governor Jelks to order a special session of the Fourth Judicial Circuit Court, but his excellency replied that he had no authority to issue such a command.

Court Officials Returning Home from Camden.

Selma, Jan. 14.—(Special.)—The grand jury empaneled by the Circuit Court convened in Camden for the special term to investigate the murder of a negro Arthur Stewart, confined in the Pineapple calaboose on December 26, 1903, was discharged by Judge John Moore last evening when, after a session of about three hours, it reported finally that it had heard the testimony adduced in the case and found no true bill.

Emmett Barlow, Evandor Melton, Walton C. Stewart, Robert Ray and Pressley Stewart who were in jail pending an investigation of the crime were by order of the court released from custody.

The court convened for its special term Monday morning when juries, grand and petit, were drawn. The grand jury was organized yesterday afternoon, fourteen men being empaneled and E. F. Oakley being chosen foreman. The jurors were in session about three hours. Their final report was that, after hearing all the evidence, they could not find true bills and the formal discharge was made by Judge Moore the presiding officer of the court.

It is rumored that the jury was divided on the question of indictments, seven standing for finding true bills against the men who were charged by the coronors jury with the murder and seven standing for adjournment without indictments.

Immediately after the final report of the grand jury had been received the five men who had been in custody for more than two weeks were ordered released and court adjourned.

Judge Moore and Solicitor Quarles came to Selma tonight.

The action of the grand jury yesterday is regarded by many as the end of the famous Pineapple case. At any successive term of the court a grand jury could bring an indictment charging a person with the murder of the negro Stewart, but this is said to be improbable. The Circuit Court's next regular term is in May.

The crime for the investigation of which the special term of the Circuit Court was ordered occurred in Pineapple on the morning of December 26, 1903. About 4 o'clock that morning the people of Pineapple were aroused by a fire that destroyed stores valued at about $35,000. It was discovered that a negro, Arthur Stewart, who had been confined in the town calaboose was dead evidently from a blow upon his head and it was suspected the jail had been set afire so that the murder would not be discovered.

At the coroner's inquest, held a few days later the jurors returned a verdict charging Emmett Barlow, Evandor Melton, Walter C. Stewart, Robert Ray and Pressley Stewart with the crime and they were arrested. Because of an unexpected dissolution of the justice court organized to give the defendants preliminary hearing they had no trial and were kept in the custody of the sheriff who removed them from Pineapple to Camden.

Judge Moore of the Fourth Judicial Circuit ordered a special term of the court to investigate the case and on Monday, January 10, it convened in Camden the county seat of Wilcox County in which Pineapple is situated. The grand jury empaneled by the court returned true bills against the five men held by the sheriff, but the indictments were quashed because of a mistaken identity, J. E. Williams serving as grand juror on a subpoena issued for his brother J. N. Williams.

Another term of the court met Monday of this week and its grand jury yesterday evening having found no true bills was discharged.

Bainbridge, Ga., July 17.—Great excitement prevailed here last night on account of an attempt probably to lynch.

Deputy Sheriff Dean, on his way home from a futile attempt to apprehend a negro wanted for assault with attempt to murder, was held up about 11 o'clock by four unknown persons and the keys of the jail were demanded from him. When he denied having them, he was ordered to procure them from the sheriff.

Becoming alarmed, he reported the matter to the sheriff, and then found the parties near the Atlantic Coast Line depot. The number had alarmingly increased and numerous threats were made.

It was at first thought that the mob wished to get a man by the name of Thrash, who eloped Tuesday evening with the wife of the foreman of the Georgia, Florida and Alabama shops, but developments proved that Bill Grant was the man wanted. Grant was sentenced to be hanged at the last term of court for the murder of Jim Bird, a white man, during the holidays. A motion for a new trial had been granted and created intense feeling in this immediate territory.

Sheriff Fordham became so alarmed at the aspect of the matter, that he requested Capt. Flemming of the military company to order out his command to protect the jail. The jail was surrounded by the armed militia, and also by a number of citizens, who had been made deputies for the occasion. Frequently the guard was alarmed by suspicious persons skirting the premises. Heavy guards will be placed on tonight.

Thomasville, July 7.—(Special.)—Sunday night a negro, Bill Davis, was whipping a negro woman on the street. Mr. Wiggins tried to stop him, but the negro cursed and abused the white people. Wiggins reported the affair to Marshall J. A. McMillan, who, with five other men, went to a cabin where Davis was to arrest him. When his ammunition was exhausted he made good his escape through a window, the posse pursuing and shooting at him.

THE ONLY DAILY NEWSPAPER IN ALABAMA
News by Anticipation.
Not long ago trouble of the customary sort occurred in Bibb county, and the newsvendor made haste to add to his dispatch, "If caught he (a negro) will be lynched." Nearly every newspaper from distant cities now comes loaded with an account of a lynching in St. Clair county, which not only did not take place, but was not even considered.

The enterprising reporter in the rural districts should pull himself up to the progress of this state. He is horribly out of date in his anticipations of lynchings. A lynching would, it is true, make more news, and a reporter could thus earn more money, but under the rule of Governor William Dorsey Jelks, a lyncher would be jailed, and it would cost him much money to say the least to recover his freedom. He may desire excitement in his neighborhood, and he may be essentially bloodthirsty, but he has no desire to gratify such propensities at high expense. He knows an indictment and a trial would confront him while Governor Jelks is in office, and he hesitates, and no lynching takes place.

All that is needed now is to bring the rustic reporter up to the situation. He is lingering in the atmosphere of former days. He will soon be called a "back number" if he does not quit adding to his dispatches, "He will be lynched if caught." As a matter of fact, no one is lynched in the law-abiding state of Alabama, where anarchy has been abolished.

The Parkersburg (W. Va.) Sentinel says: "The story from Bluefield that a negro had been skinned by an infuriated mob near there was not true, nor was there any foundation for it. The entire story was made out of the whole cloth." Some one who imagined that it would be a smart trick to gull the public probably started the story and sent it over the wires, and then laughed in his sleeves at his acuteness. He looked at it as a joke on the public.

Instead of being a joke, however, it was a gross outrage. The public mind is now in a state of peculiar sensitiveness on the subject of mob law. In such a situation every account of a lynching is liable to add to the popular excitement and arouse the passions to that white heat where they are uncontrollable. The man or set of men who for their own brutal pleasure contributes to such a situation commits a crime. The manufacturers of the West Virginia story are guilty in this way, and

they should be punished to the limit of the law.

The authors of the usual deprecatory criticisms which one reads fail to realize in the least degree the state of things to which we are steering. They talk of a "deplorably mistaken sense of justice," or something of that kind, while Mr Gilman talks of "love of bloodshed" and of "homicidal instincts," for the indulgence of which the possession of a black skin is rapidly coming to be regarded as a legitimate provocation. I find it hard to comprehend the ignorance of history and of human nature which allows people still to think negro lynching as of a transient contagion destined soon to exhaust its virulence. It is, on the contrary, a profound social disease, spreading now like forest fire, and certain to become permanently endemic in every corner of our country, North and South, unless heroic remedies are swiftly adopted to check it.

Three years ago I said that unless heroic measures were adopted we should soon have civil war between the races. The Evansville riot is an example of what we may expect to-morrow wherever negroes are numerous, and very little later in such cities as New York and Boston and Philadelphia. The North is already almost as fully inoculated as the South, and the young white American of the lower classes is being educated everywhere with appalling rapidity to understand that any negro accused of crime is public spoil, to be played with as long as the fun will last. Attempts at general massacres of negroes are certain to be the next thing in order, and collective reprisals by negroes are equally certain.

The average church-going Civilizee realizes, one may say, absolutely nothing of the deeper currents of human nature, or of the aboriginal capacity for murderous excitement which lies sleeping even in his own bosom. Religion, custom, law and education have been piling their pressure upon him for centuries mainly with the one intent that his homicidal potentialities should be kept under. The result, achieved with infinite difficulty, is the blessed public peacefulness which until recently we have enjoyed, a regimen in which the usual man forgets that in the practical sense there is any bloodthirstiness about him, and deems it an exceptional passion, only to be read about in newspapers and romances. Methodical diminution of tempting pretexts and provocations, social condemnation of violent acts, the rarity of bad examples, and the fear of the gallows, are the forces which have brought us to this tameness, which is the very triumph of our civilization.

But the water-tight compartment in which the carnivora within us is confined is artificial and not organic. It never will be organic. The slightest diminution of external pressure, the slightest loophole of licensed exception, will make the whole system leaky, and murder will again grow rampant. It is where the impulse is collective, and the murder is regarded as a punitive or protective duty, that the peril to civilization is greatest. Then, as in the hereditary vendetta, in dueling, in religious massacre, history shows how difficult it is to exterminate a homicidal custom which is once established.

Negro lynching is already a permitted exception in the midst of our civilization. Blood orgy and diseased idea emotion have struck an unholy partnership, impunity is agreed upon, and an anonymous mob is the power to which the license is accorded. The newspapers are doing all they can to convert the custom into an established institution. I first learned of the recent negro burning at Wifmington by seeing the scare bead of a paper which a man on a seat before me in a car was reading. "Charred in Chains, Lynching Well Done!" was printed in tall capitals in this Boston daily. One of our most influential New York weeklies, formerly an independent journal, printed an editorial on the same atrocity, of which the only influence on a susceptible mind could be to make it seem excusable. Everywhere we find educated men and women making light of the baseness, as being, after all, only a rude sort of justice, just as old-fashioned Christians used to say that Jews must continue to be baited for the honor of our Savior. Negro lynching claims more and more the character of a public right. It appeals to the punitive instinct, to race antipathy and to the white man's pride, as well as to the homicidal frenzy. One shudders to think what roots a custom may strike when a fierce animal appetite like this and a perverted ideal emotion combine together to defend it.

One or two real fanatics there may be in every lynching, actuated by a maniacal sense of punitive justice. They are a kind of "reversion," which civilization particularly requires to extirpate. ACTRESS, WHO CHANGED THE COLOR OF HER HAIR, SUING MISS OSTERMAN AND HER MANAGER Workmen Busy in the Vatican Getting Ready for the Solemn Assemblage of the Cardinals to Elect New Pope.
ROME, July 27.—The Vatican resembles an ant hill, so feverish is the work of preparing that part of the building set aside for the Conclave. The section destined for the Conclave comprises, on the ground floor of the Vatican, the three suites of rooms which surround the famous Court of San Damaso, the rooms under the late Pope's apartments and the tower with the rooms about the Sala Ducale. On the second floor the rooms about Loggia Raphael and the Pontifical offices, comprising all the apartments formerly occupied by Cardinal Rampolla, who has left the Vatican altogether, will be used. The whole will furnish commodious lodging for about 500 people.

Sistine Chapel for Conclave.

The Sistine Chapel, as in the case of the last conclave, will be used for the meetings of the Cardinals and the balloting. There, after three solemn funeral services, which begin Tuesday, will be erected a throne for each Cardinal. Over the thrones will be baldacchinos, or canopies, attached to the wall behind. The moment a new Pope is elected he will lower his baldacchino as a token of his new dignity, thus silently announced. The Paulin Chapel will be used for the celebration of high mass every morning of the conclave, while in the Sala Ducale will be movable altars for the masses to be celebrated every morning by each Cardinal.

Courtyard Unrecognizable.

The gendarmes and Palatine Guards will be transferred to the building in the Belvedere Courtyard, where the poor pilgrims were lodged during the last jubilee, the gendarmes' barracks being transformed into kitchens, pantries, &c. The Belvedere Courtyard will be converted into general quarters for the carpenters and other workmen. The Courtyard is quite unrecognizable. The long lines of glass windows of the Loggia Raphael have been painted up to a certain height as a precaution, and shades have been put on every window better to insure secrecy.

Assurances have been given that everything will be in readiness for Friday night, but there is much yet to be accomplished.

The Cardinals at their meeting to-day again discussed the advisability of sending a note to the powers regarding the condition of the Holy See. Some of them insisted on the necessity of not allowing the occasion to pass without again protesting against the occupation of pontifical territory by Italy, thereby showing that the Papacy is determined to maintain its claims unabated. No action was taken.

Cardinal Cavagnis, in behalf of the other cardinals, to-day drew lots for the so-called "cells," as the apartments which the cardinals are to occupy during the conclave are termed.

Cardinal Gibbons celebrated early mass in the private chapel of the Sulpicians and then drove to the Vatican, where he participated in the meeting of the Congregation of Cardinals. He was cordially received. He then took the oath of the gospels, administered by Cardinal Oregna, to maintain strict secrecy on all questions discussed at the meeting of the Congregation, and defend the rights, prerogatives and temporal claims of the Church.

When the meeting was over Cardinal Gibbons went to St. Peter's and prayed before the Blessed Sacrament. He knelt before the resting place of the body of Pope Leo and prayed for about fifteen minutes. Cardinal Gibbons has appointed Father P. C. Gavan as his conclavist beside whom he will take only one servant into the conclave.

Miss Hess, the young woman who was assaulted by Clark is this afternoon able to walk about the house and her recovery is assured. This fact, however, does not lessen the determination of the men who have been hunting for the negro and if he is found he will undoubtedly be hanged immediately.

Details of Crime.

Kahoka, July 28.—Frank Clark the half-breed who ravished Ollie, the 15-year-old daughter of Mrs. Ella Hess, a widow living two miles west of Kahoka, Saturday evening was a jockey, whose home was at Carrollton, but who had spent considerable time at Kahoka. The girl was on her way from Medill and when near her home met the negro in the public road. He passed her, then turned and followed her, and running up behind knocked her down with his fist and choked her. He then dragged her some distance up a hollow from the road. He drew a knife and threatened to cut her throat if she resisted, and to emphasize the threat, cut her neck slightly. In the struggle one of her fingers came in contact with the knife and was severely cut. When the negro released her the girl ran to the house and gave the alarm. Neighbors were aroused and Kahoka people informed of the crime. A search was instituted but the negro had made good his escape. The fire bells were rung and whistles blown in order to draw the people together, that posses might be formed to continue the search. Since then armed bodies of men have scoured the country in every direction.

Girl Will Recover.
The girl, though badly bruised and cut is able to be up and about the house. There is no doubt but that if the fiend is caught he will be hung to the nearest tree. The excitement is intense and knots of excited people are on every corner.

The latest report from Miss Hess was that she was in a fair way to recover from the injuries received. She is about seventeen years of age and is said to be a fine looking young woman. She lives with her mother who is a widow. Her father met his death by an accident six years ago. While out hunting he was instantly killed by the accidental discharge of his gun.

County Attorney Rutherford and Sheriff Arnold raised $300 by subscription among the citizens, and that amount is expected to be doubled in two or three days more. When county court meets Monday it will offer an additional $200, and the governor is expected to augment this $300 more, which will raise the reward to about $1,000. Following is a description of the fugitive issued by Sheriff Arnold:

Clark's Description.

Weight about 160 pounds; about 5 feet 5 or 6 inches tall; dark mulatto, and might be taken for a dago; heavy build and slightly stoop shouldered; coal black hair, parted in the middle. When last seen wore black moustache, cap, dark colored light-weight coat, light colored cotton pants and light colored shirt. Clothes dirty and shabby. He will attract attention wherever seen. He is a crap shooter, frequents saloons, attends the county fairs, and jockeys with race horses, and has been identified as Frank Clark, of Carrollton, Mo.

Girl Tells of Assault.

rington  Journ  July  30
Girl Tells of Assault.

Farmington, Iowa, July 30.—Miss Hess, who was assaulted by the negro, has partially recovered from her injuries and the shock. In an interview had with the girl she stated:

"I had been down to Medill to decorate the church for Sunday and was coming home with Abe Harkness in his wagon. It was about 5:30 o'clock. Abe's house is about a mile from Medill and ours is a little farther. Abe drove into his yard and I got down from the wagon and started to walk on to my house. I saw a colored man with black hair, or wool, and a heavy black mustache. a little ways behind me, but I did not suppose he would try to hurt me or I would have run home. I should think he would weigh about 140 pounds. I walked on up the road toward the house, and all of a sudden I felt something—it was his fist, I suppose—hit me in the back of the head. I looked around and saw the colored man. I tried to scream, but he grabbed me by the throat so that I could hardly get my breath. Then he took a knife or a razor and cut me in several places and threw me down. That is all I remember for a while. When I came to I was very weak, but crawled to the house and told my mother what had happened to me. My father is dead."

Chase for Criminal Begins.

As soon as the girl came home, Mrs. Hess tried to notify the authorities at Kahoka, but could not get word to them until 2 o'clock Sunday morning. The fire bells were then rung and the whistles sounded, and in a short time a mob of 700 heavily armed men was out in hot pursuit scouring the country for miles in every direction. All of the neighboring towns were notified to be on the lookout for the fugitive. Clark, whose home is at Edina, Mo., is a half-breed, being part negro and part Italian. He is a foot racer and jockey, and has appeared in races at Kahoka for several years.

Sunday afternoon about 3:30 o'clock he was seen running across the Hiller farm, which is between Kahoka and Medill, and five minutes later a party of searchers passed the same way. Monday morning it was reported that a negro answering the description given was surrounded about a mile from Medill, but he was captured and found not to be the man wanted.

Early Tuesday morning a crowd of about 300 men near Kahoka received word that another posse had captured Clark at Coffee church, between Downing and Memphis, Mo. The mob near Kahoka dispersed when this news was received, but it was later found that the report was a false one. The last time he was positively seen, Clark was taking dinner with a widow between Downing and Memphis, Monday noon. The last time seen before committing the crime was about 3:10 o'clock Saturday afternoon at Kahoka, when he said that he was going to Medill and would ride from there to his home at Edina. Henry Miller, a colored man living in Kahoka, who is said to be a bad man, was running around Saturday night trying to hire a team. His action aroused the suspicions of the citizens, and an armed guard surrounded his house.

The state of Missouri offers $500, Kahoka $200 and Clarke county $300 for the negro's arrest.

CLARK IS CAPTURED
RAVISHER OF KAHOKA, MO., GIRL UNDER ARREST IN GALES- BURG. ILLINOIS.
MAKES A FULL CONFESSION
Is Recognized By Telegraph Operator in Illinois City Who Formerly Knew Clark in Missouri Haunts—Has Had Varied Career.
Frank Clark, the negro for whom a search has been made over Iowa, Illinois and Missouri, wanted on the charge of ravishing Ollie Hess, near Kahoka, Mo., July 25, has been captured in Galesburg, Ill., and is said to have confessed to the accusation. Since the crime Ottumwa officers have been on the lookout for Clark and shortly thereafter it was reported several times that the man had been seen in this vicinity.

Officers at Galesburg were notified of his presence by a telegraph operator who formerly knew Clark in his Missouri haunts and his arrest followed shortly thereafter. Concerning the capture the Galesburg Evening Mail of Thursday says:

"Hello, Clark!" said a very tall, broad-shouldered Missourian about half-past three o'clock this morning as he stood before a cell in the Galesburg police station, confronting the man who yesterday swore to a statement that he was Frank, alias "Yellow" Clark, and that he was guilty of assaulting Ollie Hess, a 17-year-old girl, at Medill, Mo., last July.

"Hello, Mr. Arnold," was Clark's reply as he thrust his hand through the opening in the cell gate and grasped the hand of the sheriff of Clark county.

Clark is Indentified.

"That's the man," said the sheriff in an aside to Chief of Police Shadley, and inside another half hour the self-confessed criminal was on his way to the C., B. and Q. station bound for Missouri.

According to the statement of the sheriff, Clark is sure to be hung after his trial. Fearing to take his prisoner back to Clark county, the sheriff and the chief went to Palmyra, two counties distant from Clark, where the prisoner will be kept safely until the time for his trial. The sheriff declared that if he took his prisoner back to the scene of his crime now his life would not be worth a penny, as a mob would surely lynch him.

Sheriff Arnold and L. Alexander, editor of the Kahoka Review, left Kahoka yesterday expecting to arrive in Galesburg yesterday afternoon on the Santa Fe. The train was long delayed and did not arrive until after 3 o'clock this morning. The two men made their way at once to the station. Sheriff Arnold informed Chief Shadley that a deposit of $500 was waiting in a bank in his city for Officers Pontus Nelson and William Houston and Harvey Machen, who made the capture of Clark here, and that $500 more would be paid as soon as he is convicted of his crime.

Condition of the Girl.

The sheriff says that Ollie Hess was not so badly injured as at first reported. He says that there is clear proof that Clark accomplished his purpose, but that he did not cut her throat and that she was badly shocked as the result of the terrible deed. Clark, it is said, attempted to draw a knife over the girl's throat but she fought him and her hand was cut in the fight. The officer admits the feeling against Clark in Clark county is at fever heat and that if the people there should get sight of the prisoner now it would be a sure case of lynch.

That is what Clark feared most and he begged the officers here not to allow him to be taken back there. He spent almost one entire night in the station here viewing the situation in his mind. The slightest noise would cause him to cringe in his cell and he afterwards admitted that he was afraid a Galesburg mob would lynch him.

Left the County.

It is learned that after Clark assaulted the girl on July 25 he left that part of the country and working along the Santa Fe passed through Galesburg and went to Joliet. There he remained several weeks and started again for the southwest, expecting to go to Mexico. He was wont to help the railroad men in their work and as he was a good switchman he was given his passage in return for the work. It was on his way to the west that he passed through Galesburg, and while assisting the trainmen here was recognized by Harvey Machen, who at once communicated the fact to the police and his arrest followed.

Sheriff Arnold, accompanied by Chief Shadley and the prisoner; left on the early morning train for Palmyra where Clark will be placed in jail. Mr. Alexander returned home to Clark county on the Santa Fe. It is likely that the Galesburg men will receive a check for their money at once.

Mr. Alexander visited the office of the Evening Mail today and stated that Clark was well known in this part of the country. In past years the mulatto has been a race horse rider and his parents are living at Carlton, Mo. It is understood that Clark was under arrest one time at Kansas City for a crime. Mr. Alexander is strongly of the opinion that Clark will surely be hung if convicted of the crime.

frank-clark-farmington-1903-07-27.A28:
MUST HAVE JUSTICE
KAHOKA PEOPLE SAY CLARK'S TRIAL WILL BE FAIR.
VALUE GOOD NAME OF THE COUNTY
It is Expected by Many That the Prisoner Will be Condemned to Death—Great Care to be Exercised in Selecting a Jury.
Kahoka, Mo., Sept. 25.—As the time for the trial of Frank Clark, the confessed ravisher of Ollie Hess, grows nearer, the interest in it becomes more intense. Not only are the people of Clark county, Mo., interested in the now famous case, but the eyes of the people of the surrounding country will watch the case to its close. The Kahoka people speak of the matter calmly enough. There is a determined feeling that the criminal shall be accorded a fair trial. The people fully realize that violence to Clark at the hands of a mob would be a dark blot on the county's name. Every precaution will be taken to prevent any move made in the way of violence. As one prominent man of Kahoka put it: "If Clark is permitted to have a fair trial and is legally executed it will be a feather in the cap of Clark county. It will prove to the world that Missouri is not nearly as bad a place as some people would paint it. Everybody here believes that the jury will find Clark guilty of the crime charged and that he will be sentenced to death by hanging. Anything short of this will be deemed insufficient and there is no telling what may happen. The people, especially the neighbors of the Hess family, might become frenzied if Clark should only receive a penitentiary sentence, and take matters into their own hands, if possible."

Question of a Jury.

Some difficulty is expected to be experienced in the selection of a jury. The prosecuting attorney, W. T. Rutherford, said he did not anticipate a great deal of trouble in selecting a jury. The law says there must be forty qualified jurors. In a case of this kind, capital offense, the defendant is entitled to twenty peremptory challenges and the state eight peremptory challenges, making twenty-eight in all. This it will be seen, will leave the twelve jurors who will finally be selected to sit on the famous case.

Care to be Used.

The sheriff will be instructed to go to those districts of the county lying farthest away from the scene of the crime and bring in seventy-five men. If the jury cannot be selected out of this number, the sheriff will subpoena more men until the jury is selected.

It is suspected that the attorneys for the defendant will make a strong attempt to secure a change of venue on the plea that a fair trial cannot be obtained in Clark county. Such an attempt will be fought vigorously. The prosecuting attorney claims he is in a position to frustrate such a plan should the attempt be made by the defense.

Much Interest in Case.

The next term of the circuit court at Kahoka commences October 12, 1903, with Judge Ed McKee of Memphis on the bench. This case will come up soon after court convenes. Judge McKee stands high in the opinion of the bar in his circuit, comprising four counties. He metes out justice without fear or favor. It is possible that Judge McKee may not sit on the Clark case, but it is not at all probable that he will not. Should the attorney for the defense swear that Judge McKee is prejudiced in this case, he cannot preside, over it. In such an event, any circuit judge in Missouri who is idle at the time may preside. The eyes of the entire surrounding country will be upon Kahoka when Clark's trial commences and the result will be awaited with great interest.
frank-clark-farmington-1903-07-27.A30:
CLARK IS SENTENCED.
A special from Kahoka, Mo., says that Frank Clark, the confessed ravisher of Miss Olive Hess, who was found guilty by the jury in the trial at Kahoka, which terminated last Thursday with the death penalty attached, was brought before Judge McKee, who named Nov 25 as the day for his execution. Clark did not appear at all effected by this gruesome announcement which would send him into eternity, but looked up to the judge with the remark:
"Thank you, sir."

When being taken out of the court house, on his way down the aisle, he smiled blandly and did not seem to be at all disturbed, or did not realize what the near future had in store for him. He displayed wonderful nerve and seemed careless of his fate. There were no special proceedings and the closing act of the trial was soon over with only the brief talk of the judge fixing the date of execution.
frank-clark-farmington-1903-07-27.A32:
NEGRO CRIMINAL IS LEGALLY HANGED TODAY AT KAHOKA, MISSOURI.
EXECUTION HURRIED
The Authorities, Fearing That a Mob Would Break Down Stockade, Hanged Clark at 2 P. M., Today Two Hours Before Appointed Time.
Kahoka, Mo., Nov. 25.—(Special) — Fearful lest a mob should break down the stockade about the gallows in the jail yard and take matters away from the officers of the law, the authorities hastened the execution of Frank Clark the negro who assaulted Miss Ollie Hess just four months ago today was hanged at 2 o'clock this afternoon, two hours before the time announced for his execution.

Little Excitement.

Aside from the fact that the town was full of curious people many of them farmers who had driven miles to be present, Kahoka did not seem out of the ordinary this morning. About the jail where Clark was confined all was quiet but the officers in charge were fearful that it was the quiet preceding a storm and in order to prevent any possible hitch in their plans they decided early this morning to hang Clark before the time appointed for his execution. The execution was carried out according to plans with the single exception of the time and there is no excitement this afternoon.

Professed Religion.

Three weeks ago Clark, who has confessed that he is guilty of one of the most heinous crimes that has ever disgraced the history of the state of Missouri, expressed his faith in the Catholic religion. About a week ago he was baptized by Rev. Father Muckerman, pastor of the Catholic church of Kahoka, who has daily visited him as his spiritual adviser.

Grew Morose.

During the first few weeks after his being sentenced Clark displayed much bravado and repeatedly said that he would not flinch when the time came to die but during the past week he apparently began to realize the end that was in store for him and he grew morose and taciturn. This afternoon, when he was brought out to be hanged however, he was calm and apparently not unnerved and he went to his death with a bravado worthy of a better man.

After Hill had paid his fare he claimed that he had given the conductor a $5 gold piece, but the conductor claimed that he was mistaken. "When the car reached Marengo avenue Hill jumped off. The car continued its journey around the north loop and Hill met it at Worcester avenue, where he jumped aboard.

"You can give me $4.90 now and we well be square," the colored man remarked.
"Carlton denied that the colored man had any change due him, and the two men again became involved in a dispute, each insisting in the most emphatic manner that the other was in error. Carlton finally said that he did not even have a $5 gold piece in his pocket, and as he said so he stuck his hand in his pocket as if to pull out all his money and show it to his troublesome passenger. Hill thrust his right hand into one of his pockets and when he drew it out it contained a 38-calibre revolver. Without a word of warning he pointed the weapon at Carlton's stomach and pulled the trigger. Carlton fell in a heap on the platform and Hill pulled the trigger of his weapon twice, but it failed to discharge the bullet. He then jumped from the car and ran in the direction of Casterline's livery stable, but sturbled and fell. Policeman John O. Reynolds, who had heard the shot, ran toward the car, and seeing Hill running, he gave chase. The colored man arose after falling and started to run, but Reynolds grabbed him in a grip that took him clear off his feet. The officer quickly took the revolver away from him and handcuffed him and then took him to the city jail."

huse-thompson-robeline-1903-01-04.A3:
JUDGE PORTER'S CHARGE.
A Protest Against Lynching—An Appeal for Law and Order..
The charge of Judge Porter to the grand jury of Natchitoches will leave its impress on every citizen favoring not only law and order but justice. Unfortunately there are beings who assume that a nigger, like a wild beast, may be shot and killed at will for any provocation. Judge Porter condemns the mob. He upholds the law. There can be no excuse for lynching except the nameless crime. The case to which Judge Porter calls special attention is the lynching of a negro near Robeline. This negro had resisted arrest. "I am informed," says Judge Porter. "that about the 1st of this month a negro man was taken from the lock-up in the town of Robeline and, as I am informed, after being beaten in the most inhuman manner, was strangled to death by being hung to a tree. The victim of the mob in this case was not charged with that nameless crime which sometimes plunges whole communities into a frenzy of rage and brings swift justice upon the perpetrator. So you observe that the mob in this case-not only assumed the right to execute the law, but actually exercised the highest power of the sovereign, the power to make the law. The community in which this helpless prisoner was murdered—and it was murder, in the sight of God and man—is noted for its schools and churches, its Christian men and women, and its cultured society; and I am happy to say that the substantial people in that community are united in condemning the outrage."

It is not expected that the grand jury will find a bill against any one connected with this mobbing but Judge Porter's charge will have a good effect. It will at least stand as a protest against this act of the lynchers—a condemnation of an unwarranted, an illegal assumption of authority on the part of citizens who should uphold the law. Lynching can not be excused, except for the nameless crime, in a civilized community where courts and juries can dispense even-handed justice and mete out punishment commensurate to the crime committed.

NEW-ORLEANS SHIPPING TIED UP.
Lockout of Union Longshoremen by Steamship Companies.
[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]
Orleans, Sept. 16—The entire ocean

New-Orleans, Sept. 16.—The entire ocean shipping of the Port of New-Orleans, with the exception of the Southern Pacific Line of steamers, was tied up as tight as a drum to-day. This state of affairs was brought about by the lockout of all the union men on the riverfront by the steamship companies on account of the alleged violation of the agreement under which the recent strike was settled by the longshoremen's unions.

There was a riotous scene this morning at the wharf where the coffee ship Canaries is being unloaded. Some of the negro longshoremen were not pleased with the action of the unions and attempted to go to work, when a crowd of strikers appeared and drove them from the docks. The police interfered, whereupon the strikers turned upon the officers and steamship agents and newspaper reporters who were present, and threatened to throw them into the river. Chairman Moriarity, of the longshoremen's strike committee, harangued the strikers and urged them to buy Winchesters and shotguns and take charge of the wharves by force of arms and hold the riverfront. The police turned in a riot call, and a large force of officers responded and dispersed the strikers.

The members of the unions are split up into factions over the trouble with the ship agents, and a collision between the union men was narrowly averted later in the day. The executive committee of the colored longshoremen's union was bitterly denounced by a crowd of white union men and the members of the committee were forced to flee to escape a beating. Threats were made by union men to lynch J. B. Williams, the president of the colored longshoremen's union. These threats were made by white longshoremen, and had the effect of causing the negroes to rally to the support of their chief. The steamship agents declare they will fight the unions to a finish, and negotiations have been opened with labor agencies to supply them with three thousand men immediately.

CONSTABLE SCHULTZ'S FEAT.

As an outcome of the shooting of Conductor William Smith on the Louisville and Eastern electric road Saturday night, Jim Nichols, colored was shot and perhaps fatally wounded yesterday morning by Constable Hugo Schultz, of St. Matthews. Before the bullet was fired Schultz had a desperate struggle with the negro for the possession of the revolver, and it was only after he had been fired upon that he shot. He arrested Will Nicholas after an exciting scene.

Conductor William Smith was shot Saturday night at Houston's, a small station beyond Anchorage. Will Nichols, a negro, boarded the car in Louisville, and soon after the car started on its trip he began to raise a disturbance. Other negroes joined in. Smith ordered them to remain quiet. Instead Nichols became all the more abusive in his remarks to the passengers. Again Smith ordered him to remain quiet. The demands of the conductor were ignored, and as a last resort he was compelled to eject Nichols and three others from the car at Houston's. Nichols was under the influence of liquor, and as he was thrown off the car he threatened to shoot Smith. When Pewee Valley was reached Smith secured a revolver from one of his friends, believing that the negro would attempt to carry out his threats.

As the car reached Houston's on its return to this city the ten passengers were startled by loud reports of pistol shots. Two of the bullets crashed through the car. When the smoke had cleared away it was found that Smith had been wounded. He was shot in the thigh. He gamely continued on the car until the car barn was reached and then his wounds were dressed. Later he was brought to this city and taken to his home at Twenty-eighth street and Portland avenue. The wound is not of a dangerous nature. Smith said the four negroes flagged the car as Houston's was reached; that he was assaulted by one of them as he stepped on the platform, as is his custom, to help passengers. Some one from behind knocked him down. Fortunately he fell on the car steps and hung there. Will Nichols, he says, fired three shots. The first two went through the car windows and the third struck the helpless conductor. The latter drew his pistol, but the trigger snapped fire and the negroes thus escaped.

Constable Schultz heard about the shooting late Saturday night. Yesterday morning he left St. Matthews on one of the early cars in an effort to locate Nichols, and he had been searching only a short time before he found out that the negro could be located at a little cabin near Brownsboro, in Oldham county. When Schultz reached the cabin the door was barred. Repeated knocks brought no response. Schultz walked around to one of the windows of the cabin and looked in. Five large negroes were in the room. Two were the Nichols brothers. The other three were not recognized by the Constable. Schultz then made known his business. The negroes made no reply. Schultz walked around to the door. It had been unbolted and he walked in. As soon as he stepped inside Jim Nichols jumped at him. Schultz drew his revolver and Jim Nichols grabbed the weapon, and a struggle commenced for possession. During the struggle the pistol was discharged, the ball passing close to Schultz's hip. Schultz wrenched the revolver from the negro's hand and fired. The bullet entered Nichols' left breast.

During the entire struggle Will Nichols had remained inactive. He had remained inside of the cabin. As he saw that his brother had been shot he ran to one end of the cabin and secured a shotgun. He rushed to the door of the cabin and opened fire. Schultz escaped unhurt, and after the negro had emptied the contents of the gun he returned fire. Nichols closed the door and declared that he would never be taken alive. People living in the neighborhood had been attracted to the scene by the shooting.

Messengers were dispatched to Pewee Valley for Town Marshal Marion Spears. Constable Ad Hall, of Oldham county, was also notified. In a short time both of the men and a posse of twenty-five arrived on the scene. For a time it seemed that mob violence would gain the better of the posse, but the efforts of the officers were united in trying to restrain the men. Finally Nichols appeared at the window and announced that he would surrender if protection was given him. This was agreeable to the officers. Nichols opened the door and was taken in charge by the officers. He was handcuffed and brought to jail on the 11 o'clock car and was charged with malicious shooting with intent to kill.

Jim Nichols was found to be in a serious condition. The ball entered his left lung. Dr. R. B. Pryor was hastily summoned. The condition of the negro is serious and the chances are not favorable to his recovery.

LOGANSPORT, Ind., July 28.—A pack of bloodhounds from the Fort Wayne police department arrived this afternoon to be placed on the track of the unknown man who assaulted Mrs. Joseph Watts on the highway near her home in Harrison township, this county, last night, and in search of whom an armed posse of farmers in that locality spent nearly all last night and this morning. So far no trace of the assailant has been found, and this afternoon the bloodhounds were taken out to the Watts farm to take the scent from the footprints the man left in the road. Men have been stationed along the railroads and highways in the vicinity, and excitement has been raging high among the farmers of that locality.

Mrs. Watts was attacked last night after dark on her return from the residence of her son, George Watts, a half mile distant. When several hundred feet from her own home a man who had been sitting under a tree along the roadside, sprang out at her and seizing her about the throat choked her and threw her down. She screamed and her cries were heard by her younger son, Frank Watts, who was in the barnyard nearby. Seizing his rifle, he ran to her assistance. The assailant released his hold upon the woman and sprang across the road into a corn field, where he disappeared. Young Watts fired two shots after him, but neither had any effect. Search has been made for the man but without avail.

For the description given by Mrs. Watts, her assailant was either a very light colored negro or a dark complexioned white man. Mrs. Watts was rendered unconscious by the vicious attack of the brute, but he failed to do her much injury. Several bruises were left on her neck and throat from the effect of his fierce attack, but otherwise she is uninjured. Indignation is said to be run very high in the community.

Five negroes were implicated in the shooting, which will probably result fatally.

THREE COLORED MEN LYNCHED.
PHIL DAVIS, WALTER CARTER and CLINT THOMAS, colored men, were lynched near Balcher, Louisiana, which is twenty miles from Shreveport, Nov. 30th upon the charge of having fatally shot a white man named ROBERT ADGER. Twelve hundred white and colored people witnessed the execution, which partook of the nature of a picnic. Colored men are alleged to have taken a part in the man hunt and so valuable were the services of one of them in this particular that he was presented with a purse of $100. This is the peculiar part of southern life. We do not know of a Negro k liling of this sort, but what some other Negro did not make himself one of the leading characters in hunting the alleged culprit to his death.

Some people would naturally conclude that this would have a tendency to relieve the colored people in that locality of all responsibility for the action of the guilty party, but it does not. On the other hand, the Negro-haters become more intolerant and it is not many days or weeks before some overt act on the part of the white hoodlums precipitates more blood-shed with the consequent slaughter of the innocent. What excuse can be given for this murderous violation of the law on the part of the mob? It is admitted that both white and colored people were bitterly against the culprits and that the juries in this locality are composed exclusively of white men. These colored men had absolutely no chance to escape and their execution by due process of law was a foregoing conclusion.

Colored people cannot afford to be parties to such lawlessness and it is to be regretted that in yielding to the prevailing sentiment, they condoned an act which was nothing more nor less than murder. The lynchers are now guilty of the same crime with which their victims stood charged. There were no white ladies to be forced into court and make a graphic recital of their shame. It was a plain case of shooting with fatal results. Colored men, who surrender to mobs take their lives in their own hands. Death by a straight stand-up and knock down fight is always preferable to this slow, strangling process from the limb of a tree Lynch-law must go!

Death of Mr. Robert E. Adger.
Mr. Robert E. Adger, who was shot by negroes November 28th, at Belcher, died on the 7th instant. Hope against hope had filled the hearts of his fond wife and devoted relatives and friends for his recovery, and all was done that could be done, but to no avail.

Mr. Adger was a son of Mr. Joseph Ellison Adger, deceased, one of Bossier's most eminent citizens; was about 46 years of age, and spent most of his life in this parish, where he was well and favorably known, and had many warm friends. He was a prominent planter and merchant and leading citizen.

Deceased leaves a wife and two small daughters, Mamie and Bessie; two brothers, Messrs. Joseph E. and Wm. L. Adger, and other relatives, to mourn his death, and to whom the Banner extenes its sincerest sympathy.

The funeral services were held by Rev. W. A. Zeigler and Rev. Mr. Woodbridge Monday evening, in the presence of a very large number of friends, and the remains interred at Cottage Grove cemetery.

— United States Senator Asbury C. Latimer of South Carolina addressed the Southeastern Iowa Good Roads Association at Burlington, one afternoon last week. He favored government aid in highway improvement. He said: "An effort is now being made by some of the most influential men in public life to devise some financial scheme by which the treasury surplus now taken from circulation under the Dingley tariff may be put back into circulation. The scheme is to loan this money to national banks without interest. I am opposed to this and feel it would be better for the Federal government to appropriate $100,000,000 of this surplus per annum for five years for building good roads. This $500,-000,000, supplemented by an additional $500,000,000 from the people, would, in my judgment, meet all the demands necessary to improve the roads throughout the Union. The result would be an increased value of land throughout the United States anywhere from 10 to 50 per cent, on 6,000,-000 acres of tillable land."

— Trial by jury in civil actions in the county courts in England has long been declining in popularity. On one circuit, in which several thousand cases of some importance were disposed of during 1902, not a single action was tried with a jury. This is certainly not surprising, if county juries often behave as did the five good men and true whose strange methods in arriving at a verdict were described by a county court judge in the London Times the other day. The case, which arose out of an accident, lasted two days. "The jury of five retired. Said No. 1: 'Oil, Grease & Oil are my solicitors; my verdict is for them. Oddly enough, No. 2 and No. 3 also employed the same solicitors, and so the three were solid for Oil, Grease & Oil. For hours Nos. 4 and 5 held out. Night was far advanced; they were cold and hungry and submitted." This is bad enough, but what the county court judge adds is even more calculated to make all litigants' flesh creep. "Up spake No. 1: 'Let me see, were Oil, Grease & Oil for plaintiff or defendant?' But, alas! none of the five knew."
